examples.question_text:
Seven of eight equal sections of a tank hold $77$ L.
(a) Find the capacity of the tank.
(b) How many more litres are needed to fill it?
examples.solution_text:
(a) One section: $77\div7=11$ L
Eight sections: $11\times8=88$ L
The capacity is $88$ L.
(b) One of the eight sections is empty.
$88-77=11$ L
Another $11$ L is needed.

examples.question_text:
$\frac{5}{6}$ of a number exceeds $\frac{1}{6}$ of it by $36$.
(a) Find the number.
(b) Check the stated difference.
examples.solution_text:
(a) The difference is four sixths of the number.
One sixth: $36\div4=9$
Six sixths: $9\times6=54$
The number is $54$.
(b) Five sixths: $9\times5=45$
One sixth: $9$
$45-9=36$, as stated.

examples.derivation: Two thirds represent 26 cm, so one third is 26 ÷ 2 = 13 cm and the whole is 13 × 3 = 39 cm. Multiplying 26 directly by 3 omits finding one third. Both diagrams have three equal sections; the question labels only the known two-thirds amount, while the solution labels each section 13 cm and the whole 39 cm. This follows the unitary method explicitly supplied in Mixed Practice Q6 and Challenge Exercise Q1–2.
